changes.after: Single quotes name one ordinary character value. The %c format prints it as a character.

before: An ordinary single-quoted character constant such as 'A' has type int in C. A double-quoted literal is an array of char ending in a zero character.
char need not be signed on every implementation. Its value is not automatically a whole Unicode character in a multibyte encoding.
printf %c receives an int and writes the corresponding character after conversion. Do not assume alphabetic letters have particular numeric codes.
The example changes a character constant rather than depending on ASCII arithmetic.
Expected output or behavior: A. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare %c output with a double-quoted message. Do not infer universal encoding numbers from one system. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: `'A'` is a character constant: a value written with single quotes. In C, this ordinary constant has type int. Double quotes make a string instead: an array of char values ending in zero.
A char stores one byte. Text such as some accented letters or emoji can need several bytes. Do not assume one char always holds one whole visible symbol.
`%c` expects an int value and prints its character after conversion to unsigned char. It does not print the number as decimal digits.
Different systems can use different character codes. Write the character you mean in single quotes instead of guessing its number. This example names A directly.
The program stores the value for A and prints A, followed by a newline.
Replace the single-quoted A with a single-quoted B. The format stays `%c` because you still want a character.
